author: Paul Purcell & Roger Franklin
title: Hanson 1, Hacks 0
text:
Hanson 1, Hacks 0
Thirty years of surviving contempt, ridicule and derision left her in no doubt what to expect from the Canberra’s arrogant and insular gallery and she didn’t hesitate to hit back hard and often. From the get go, it was clear she wouldn’t be putting up with nonsense. “Don’t expect a divisive welcome to country from me,” she began. Instead, she delivered her own welcome, one that set the theme of her appearance: we should treat Australians as one rather than dividing us into neat categories defined by indigeneity, ethnicity, and identity.
She was only warming up when a large yellow banner purporting to demonstrate her hypocrisy began to scroll down behind her. “Find that person and sack them!” someone cried, presumably a One Nation supporter, as Press Club staffers tore down the banner. David Sharaz, aka Mr Brittany Higgins, of GetUp! was seen to film the whole debacle and then bolt from the room like an overweight cat with a stolen sausage. Reports suggest Australian Federal Police investigators are very keen to have an extended word with Sharaz, perhaps to convey concerns that GetUp’s sophomoric prank might encourage the next harassers to plant a bomb rather than a billboard.
Hanson was unfazed. She turned to look at the poster, gave an bemused smile and continued with her speech. As she went through her policies she made it clear who she was and what she stood for, all of it summed up by her observation: “Western civilisation and its values are under siege.”
She noted how multiculturalism’s enforced relativism had made “shitholes” of Britain, Canada, Germany and France because they were afraid to confront extremism, prosecute the hate preachers and deport them. That same cowardice applies in Australia, she continued, allowing Islamic extremism to flourish “in some Sydney mosques”.
Another target at which she took aim was transgender ideology — and she didn’t hold back. Quoting Germaine Greer, Hanson reminded her audience that Australia’s foremost feminist had said that sex is tied to the body, not identity. “Just because you lop off your penis and wear a dress,” she began, quoting Greer, “doesn’t make you a woman!” It was perhaps the one moment of her address that fell short of what it might have been because there is an even better Greer quote: “I’ve asked my doctor to give me long ears and liver spots and I’m going to wear a brown coat but that won’t turn me into a f*ing cocker spaniel” The Human Rights Commissioner she dismissed as an activist who would be fired under a One Nation government.
By now, Hanson was getting into her stride. She informed the audience that “If I sound defiant – yes, I am.” And she had a few more targets to take out. The National Indigenous Affairs Agency would be defunded under a One Nation government, SBS would be closed and the ABC carved into two distinct entities — a free-to-air rural broadcaster and, in the Big Smoke, a subscription service.
Then came the questions, most of them relatively polite and handled by the woman behind the lectern with a confident aplomb. When one wit asked if Australia risked being “swamped” by Muslim migration, she shot back: “Not if I’ve got any say in it. It’s radical Islam that is my grave concern.”But there were also those in the audience hostile to Pauline and she knew who they were. When The Guardian‘s Sarah Martin took the microphone to ask her gotcha question the camera flashed briefly to Hanson’s face. It wore an expression of deadly intent you might expect to observe in a kookaburra about to swoop on a snake.
Martin had written numerous articles about One Nation’s alleged internal divisions, finances and party organisation, once even claiming there was a genuine, bona fide, absolutely-no-mistake Nazi working as a One Nation policy guru. That story turned out to be false and The Guardian had to retract the claim. Undaunted by that blunder, Martin yesterday went after Hanson’s family, all but asserting she shoe-horned her daughter into a $150,000 job with One Nation’s senator Sean Bell (NSW).
Hanson rounded on her young and blonde inquisitor and went in for the kill. Martin is a dreadful reporter, she said, a low hack who would get no interviews nor be allowed to attend press conferences. This was one of those moments when Hanson defined what makes her so different. How many times have you witnessed Coalition members meekly accept being verballed, misquoted, interrupted and ‘corrected’ by the likes of, say, Their ABC’s Sarah Ferguson? Perhaps there’s a streak of masochistic kink at work: they must really enjoy being ritually humiliated to keep playing the patsy in legacy media’s game. But not Hanson, who administered a whipping to remember. “I’ve never seen a person that’s such a trashy journalist,” she snapped, saying her daughter had won the job on merit not nepotism.
After wiping the floor with Martin, it was a SBS reporter’s turn. “Shouldn’t SBS viewers have programs in their own language so they can assimilate?” she was asked. No, Hanson replied, they should be speaking English. “I understand your question,” she said to the SBS operative while wearing an expression not far removed from murderous intent: “You will be out of a job!”
Hours before Hanson’s appearance, the Nine comics’ James Massola wondered if she could pass the Press Club’s test of her ability to face tough questions.
Pass? She so far exceeded that KPI that it was possible, just possible, to picture her standing at the Dispatch Box.
